question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 3\pi $ ?
question.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}).
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi }\sqrt{{(2{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}+{(-2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }\sqrt{{cos}^{6}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$
